title: Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 TCC) SR&ED Case
subject: Remote Software Testing on a Foreign Mainframe as SR&ED Carried On in Canada
keyPhrase: Data Kinetics v The Queen 1998 TCC
summary: Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (1998, Tax Court of Canada) confirms that Canadian taxpayers testing software remotely from Canada on a foreign mainframe carry on SR&ED in Canada under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, and that a dedicated telephone line used solely for that testing is a lease of equipment claimable under the proxy method.
metaDescription: Examine the 1998 TCC ruling for Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2226) regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2226, 98 D.T.C. 1877 (Docket: 95-456-IT-G), rendered on July 28, 1998, by Justice Lucie Lamarre, stands as a foundational authority within Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence. The ruling addresses two recurring points of friction between innovative Canadian enterprises and the tax administration (formerly Revenue Canada, now the Canada Revenue Agency or CRA): first, the territorial requirement under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"), that SR&ED be "carried on in Canada" when experimental testing utilizes computer hardware physically situated in a foreign jurisdiction; and second, the statutory boundary under the proxy method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act) between excluded indirect overhead expenditures and claimable direct expenditures for the "lease of equipment".
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The appellant, Data Kinetics Ltd., was a Canadian software engineering corporation incorporated under the laws of Ontario on December 20, 1977, with its offices located in Ottawa, Ontario. During its taxation years ending January 10, 1993, and December 31, 1993 (the January 10, 1993 year-end being a deemed year-end arising from its amalgamation with Aratek International Inc.), Data Kinetics was engaged in the research and development of advanced data management and memory management software systems for large mainframe computers.

The software was written and developed by Data Kinetics' personnel at its premises in Ottawa. However, verifying the technological hypotheses and resolving the system-level uncertainties inherent in the software required testing the software on a mainframe computer that provided the full range of available operating systems, so that the software could be shown to function equally well in all of them. Because mainframes are prohibitively expensive, Data Kinetics did not own its own mainframe computer, and no Canadian service bureau was willing to rent it access for its purposes (its experimental work risked causing serious malfunctions in the operating system of a shared mainframe); the corporation therefore entered into an agreement, effective November 1, 1991, with Mantissa Corporation ("Mantissa"), an Alabama corporation whose principal place of business was located in Birmingham, Alabama. Mantissa owned and operated a suitable mainframe computer in Birmingham and agreed to furnish Data Kinetics with access to that mainframe in exchange for a monthly fee for the right to use it.

Crucially, Data Kinetics did not relocate its software engineers to Alabama to conduct the experimental testing. Instead, the appellant's engineering personnel remained physically in Ottawa and executed all testing protocols remotely from Canada. To facilitate this remote execution, Data Kinetics leased a dedicated point-to-point telephone telecommunications line linking its Ottawa development facility directly to Mantissa's mainframe computer in Birmingham. All machine instructions, test compilations, and diagnostic data were transmitted back and forth between Ottawa and Birmingham along this dedicated line. In its taxation year ended December 31, 1993, Data Kinetics paid $26,203 to Unitel in communication charges for the dedicated telephone line; separately, it made monthly-fee payments for the use of Mantissa's mainframe computer ($63,516 in the year ended January 10, 1993 and $165,157 in the year ended December 31, 1993) and paid salaries and wages to its Ottawa-based employees working on testing; no travel or lodging expenses were at issue, because no employee of Data Kinetics ever went to the U.S. to facilitate the testing.

In filing its corporate income tax returns, Data Kinetics claimed current SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the Act and corresponding Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) pursuant to subsection 127(5) and section 127.1. For the calculation of its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, for its taxation year ending December 31, 1993, the appellant elected to use the proxy method pursuant to clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act (available for taxation years ending after December 2, 1992), computing a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"), in lieu of itemizing indirect overhead expenditures.
The Minister's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") reassessed Data Kinetics and disallowed a substantial portion of the claimed SR&ED expenditures and ITCs based on two distinct legal theories. First, the Minister advanced a territorial severance argument under subsection 37(1), contending that because Mantissa's mainframe computer was physically situated in Birmingham, Alabama, the portion of the testing actually performed by the mainframe (the running of the programs on it) was SR&ED carried on outside Canada, and that using an electronic link instead of sending employees to the U.S. made no difference. While subsection 37(2) of the Act permits a current income deduction for expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada, expenditures deducted under subsection 37(2) do not enter the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, cannot be included in the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount, and do not give rise to the investment tax credit under sections 127 and 127.1 (including the refundable credit). Consequently, the Minister favoured splitting the testing expenditures into geographic components—reclassifying the mainframe usage payments to Mantissa ($63,516 and $165,157) from subsection 37(1) to subsection 37(2), while allowing under subsection 37(1) all other testing-related expenditures, including the wages and salaries of the employees working on testing (the $26,203 communication charges were disallowed on the separate proxy-method ground described below).

Second, the Minister challenged the $26,203 communication charges as excluded overhead under the proxy method pursuant to clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act. The Minister asserted that because Data Kinetics had elected to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the proxy method, the effect of the election was to limit the expenditures qualifying as SR&ED, so that any expenditure constituting overhead was excluded from the deductible SR&ED pool and already compensated through the notional PPA. According to the Minister's characterization, the $26,203 paid for the dedicated telephone line was attributable to the use of the leased Mantissa mainframe, and thus constituted overhead (with the line itself being general office equipment), as opposed to an eligible expenditure for the "lease of equipment".
Governing Statutory Framework

The dispute in Data Kinetics required the Tax Court of Canada to interpret the interlocking architecture of Section 37 and Section 127 of the Act alongside Part XXIX of the Regulations. Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature made on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Conversely, subsection 37(2) of the Act governs current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada, providing a current deduction from business income without conferring eligibility for the investment tax credit under sections 127 and 127.1. At the time of the dispute, Regulation 2900(1) (subsequently codified in subsection 248(1) of the Act) defined "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development to achieve technological advancement—and included specified support work (such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research) where such work was commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core experimental activity.

The mechanics of expenditure calculation depend heavily on whether the taxpayer elects the traditional method or the proxy method. Where a taxpayer elects the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act, deductible SR&ED expenditures are strictly restricted to specifically enumerated direct categories: subclauses (I) and (VI) cover current expenditures for the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment (other than general purpose office equipment or furniture, or "GPOEF") that are all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) or primarily (more than 50%) attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; subclause (II) covers SR&ED contracts; subclause (IV) covers directly engaged salary or wages; and subclause (V) covers materials consumed or transformed. All other overhead and indirect costs—which would otherwise be claimable under the traditional method via subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c) if directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED—are excluded from the expenditure pool under the proxy method and replaced for ITC calculation purposes by the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4).

Practitioners evaluating Data Kinetics in the contemporary Canadian tax landscape must also account for the statutory evolution of lease expenditures over the past decade. Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii) of the Act excluded any expenditure for the use of, or the right to use, property that would be capital property if owned by the claimant, temporarily eliminating equipment lease claims from the SR&ED regime. However, for expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, Parliament restored the eligibility of SR&ED lease expenditures (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3, assented to March 26, 2026) under both the traditional method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II)) and the proxy method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)), prompting the CRA to explicitly reaffirm and apply the judicial principles of Data Kinetics in its revised SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) (the Lease Expenditures Policy).
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Lamarre allowed Data Kinetics' appeals, with costs, in respect of all the expenditures in issue—the mainframe payments to Mantissa ($63,516 and $165,157), which had been reallocated to subsection 37(2), and the $26,203 dedicated telephone line expenditure (the testing salaries had already been allowed by the Minister and were not in dispute). Adopting the holistic analytical framework established by Judge Bell in Tigney Technology Inc. v. The Queen, 97 D.T.C. 414 (T.C.C.) (reversed on the territorial issue by the Federal Court of Appeal in Canada v. Tigney Technology Inc., February 7, 2000, Dockets A-70-97 and A-303-97), Justice Lamarre held that an SR&ED project must be evaluated as an integrated whole rather than artificially fractured into isolated geographic sub-steps. Because the software was designed in Ottawa and all testing instructions and data were transmitted and analyzed by employees physically working in Ottawa, the remote utilization of the Alabama mainframe formed part of a set of interrelated activities collectively necessary to advance the technology in Canada under subsection 37(1). Furthermore, Justice Lamarre ruled that the $26,203 paid for the dedicated telephone line was not to be treated differently from the payments for the use of the mainframe, which were attributable to the lease of equipment: because the parties admitted that the line was used solely to transmit data between Ottawa and the Mantissa mainframe and it formed a necessary part of the SR&ED activity, the expenditure was not for general purpose office equipment and was wholly attributable to equipment or facilities used for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, so that it fell within subsection 37(1) notwithstanding the election under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B).
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

Although Data Kinetics Ltd. ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court on the primary statutory interpretation issues regarding remote mainframe testing and dedicated telecommunications bandwidth, the reassessment and ensuing litigation arose from the Minister's competing interpretation of subsections 37(1) and 37(2) and of the proxy election, not from any characterization, contractual, or evidentiary deficiency identified by the Court. Furthermore, the decision—when read alongside the subsequent Federal Court of Appeal ruling in LGL Limited v. The Queen (2000) and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (October 14, 2022) (the Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy) and Lease Expenditures Policy—exposes four critical legal and evidentiary failure modes that routinely disqualify Canadian SR&ED claims.
Accounting and Contractual Mischaracterization of Dedicated Bandwidth as Generic Utility Overhead Under the Proxy Method

The primary catalyst for the disallowance of the $26,203 expenditure was the appellant's election of the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B): the decision records that it was because of this election that the Minister disallowed the communication charges. In the decision, the expenditure is described as "communication charges" for a "telephone line". Under Canadian tax accounting principles and the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (Section 4.7.1), payments for the use of a telephone, cellular telephone, or the Internet are generally ordinary business expenses rather than directly related SR&ED expenditures—although the same section, citing Data Kinetics, treats an expenditure for a dedicated telecommunications line as an expenditure for the lease of equipment. When a claimant elects the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), all indirect overhead is statutorily barred from being claimed as a direct SR&ED expenditure because it is notionally represented by the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA).

The decision does not indicate whether Data Kinetics had a written equipment lease agreement for the telephone line identifying any physical chattels; it records only that the appellant paid $26,203 to Unitel for the dedicated line. To overcome the Minister's presumption that a "telephone line" is a service utility rather than leased equipment, the taxpayer did not adduce technical evidence of the telecommunications architecture; rather, both parties admitted that the line was used solely for the purpose of transmitting data between the appellant's place of business in Canada and the Mantissa mainframe computer. Justice Lamarre relied on the Black's Law Dictionary definition of lease, under which when used with reference to tangible personal property, the word "lease" means a contract by which one owning such property grants to another the right to possess, use, and enjoy it for a specified period of time in exchange for periodic payment of a stipulated price, referred to as rent.

The decision itself did not address any conceptual gap between paying for intangible "bandwidth time" and leasing "tangible personal property". Data Kinetics succeeded because the Court held that the wording of clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) does not suggest that payments for the use of the mainframe and for the use of the line carrying data to and from it should be treated differently, a reading supported by the February 1994 Department of Finance Technical Note; the proposition that dedicated bandwidth can only be made available through highly sophisticated optoelectronic equipment does not appear in the judgment, but in the CRA's later application of the case in Section 4.3.1 of its Lease Expenditures Policy. The Court did not have to decide how a shared, non-dedicated line (such as a standard commercial internet connection or dial-up utility line) would be treated; its conclusion that the expenditure was not for general purpose office equipment and was wholly attributable to SR&ED in Canada rested on the parties' admission that the line was used solely to transmit data to and from the Mantissa mainframe and formed a necessary part of the SR&ED activity, so a shared line would raise all-or-substantially-all and GPOEF questions under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) that the decision did not resolve.
Informal Cross-Border Hardware Access and the Territorial Severance Trap (Subsection 37(1) vs. Subsection 37(2))

A second point of contention concerned the use of the foreign mainframe computer and the resulting dispute over the geographical locus of the SR&ED activity. As noted in the judgment, Mantissa was an Alabama corporation that owned a mainframe in Birmingham and had no objection to the appellant testing its software on that mainframe, and the parties entered into a written agreement, effective November 1, 1991, under which Mantissa furnished access to its mainframe for a monthly fee. The Minister's challenge did not turn on the form of that arrangement: the Minister treated the physical location of the mainframe processor in Alabama as proof that the testing activity itself was "carried on outside Canada" under subsection 37(2). At paragraph 39 of the decision, Justice Lamarre specifically noted that the Minister appeared to favour the splitting of the testing expenditures between those in respect of work executed in Canada and those in respect of work executed outside Canada.

While Justice Lamarre rejected this territorial splitting by invoking Judge Bell's view in Tigney Technology Inc. that an SR&ED project must be viewed as a whole under Regulation 2900, subsequent appellate jurisprudence reveals how perilous this evidentiary posture is for Canadian claimants. Less than two years after Data Kinetics, the Federal Court of Appeal in LGL Limited v. The Queen (Docket A-139-99, February 7, 2000; affirming 99 D.T.C. 675 (T.C.C.)) restricted the "project as a whole" doctrine. The Federal Court of Appeal held that looking at the project as a whole applies only at the initial threshold stage of determining whether the overall endeavour meets the definition of SR&ED under Regulation 2900 (now subsection 248(1)). Once a project is determined to be SR&ED, each constituent activity and expenditure must still be separately evaluated under subsections 37(1) and 37(2) to determine whether that specific work was physically carried on inside or outside Canada.

Crucially, in LGL Limited (at paragraph 53 of the Tax Court judgment), the Tax Court (Bowman T.C.J.) distinguished Data Kinetics on a narrow evidentiary ground (although on appeal the Federal Court of Appeal went further and expressly stated that it could not agree with the decisions in Data Kinetics and Tigney Technology Inc.): in Data Kinetics, the only element outside Canada was the passive mainframe hardware and dedicated telephone line, whereas all human agency—writing test scripts, transmitting instructions, controlling compilation runs, and evaluating output data—was physically performed by employees sitting in Ottawa. By contrast, where human personnel physically travel outside Canada to collect data or conduct testing (as occurred in LGL Limited), or where a foreign entity's personnel actively execute the testing protocols abroad, the activity is severed under subsection 37(2) and disqualified from ITCs, subject only to the narrow 10% permissible foreign salary rule subsequently enacted in subsection 37(1.4). Data Kinetics' agreement with Mantissa was not the cause of the reassessment: it already provided for a monthly fee for the right to use the mainframe, the Court accepted that the payments for the use of the mainframe were attributable to the lease of equipment, and the Minister's position rested solely on the fact that a component of the testing involved the use of a computer located outside Canada.
Confounding Proxy-Excluded Travel, Lodging, and Reimbursed Customer-Site Testing Expenditures

The third area, which was not at issue in Data Kinetics itself (no employee of the appellant ever went to the U.S., and no travel, lodging, or reimbursed expenditures were in dispute), involves ancillary testing expenditures, specifically travel and lodging expenses incurred to test software at remote or customer locations, and expenditures subject to third-party reimbursement. In its Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (Section 4.7.2, "Expenses for travel to and lodging in Canada to do testing at a customer location"), the CRA addresses travel and lodging expenses reimbursed to employees conducting experimental trials at a supplier's premises in Canada; notably, the CRA cites Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1877, not in Section 4.7.2 but in Section 4.7.1, in support of treating an expenditure for a dedicated telecommunications line as an expenditure for the lease of equipment. This topic, although outside the dispute decided in Data Kinetics, highlights a dual statutory failure mode involving both the proxy method overhead exclusion and the reimbursement clawback rules.

When a taxpayer elects the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), travel and lodging expenses incurred by employees to perform testing—even when conducted entirely within Canada at a customer site or remote testbed—cannot be claimed as deductible SR&ED expenditures or qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Because travel and lodging are neither salaries and wages under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) nor leased equipment or facilities under subclauses (I) and (VI), they constitute overhead expenditures that are statutorily replaced by the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Claimants under the proxy method who include testing travel and lodging on Form T661 suffer automatic disallowance. Furthermore, even where a claimant elects the traditional method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)—where travel and lodging expenses to perform testing at a customer location in Canada can qualify as overhead if "directly related" and "incremental" to the prosecution of SR&ED—any portion of those expenditures reimbursed by the customer or another party fails the requirement that the expenditure be borne by the claimant, or triggers reductions under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9). Moreover, if the testing at a customer location lacks contemporaneous experimental documentation distinguishing systematic hypothesis validation from routine commercial installation, debugging, or customer acceptance testing, the entire expenditure is disqualified.
Deficient Contemporaneous Usage Logs for Equipment Operating Time (ASA and Primarily Thresholds)

Under the proxy method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)), proving that an arrangement constitutes a "lease of equipment" (and not GPOEF) is only half of the statutory requirement. The claimant must also prove the proportion of the equipment's operating time attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada. To claim 100% of the lease cost, the equipment must be used "all or substantially all" (ASA, defined as 90% or more of total operating time) for SR&ED in Canada; to claim 50% of the lease cost under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI), the equipment must be used "primarily" (more than 50% of total operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. If SR&ED usage is 50% or less, zero lease expenditure is permitted under the proxy method.

As emphasized in Section 5.1 of the CRA's Lease Expenditures Policy, claimants should be able to support actual use with documentation such as lease agreements, logbooks, or other records substantiating the exact SR&ED operating time of leased equipment and bandwidth for the period. In Data Kinetics, usage was not contested: both parties admitted that the communication line was used solely for transmitting data between the appellant's Canadian place of business and the Mantissa mainframe, and the witness testimony recorded in the decision (from the appellant's president, Mr. William Olders, and Mr. Peter Green, manager of a Canada-based mainframe computer) concerned why no suitable mainframe could be found in Canada, not reconstructed usage records.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement examined in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (and its interpretive lineage in Tigney Technology Inc., LGL Limited, and current CRA policies) against the taxpayer's structural or evidentiary vulnerability and the governing judicial standard of proof.

headers: Taxpayer's Vulnerability / Basis of Minister's Challenge
Court's Standard of Proof & Governing Judicial Holding

cells: ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i) vs. s. 37(2); s. 127(9)

Territorial Nexus ("Carried on in Canada"): Current expenditures must be for SR&ED carried on in Canada to enter the s. 37(1) pool, form part of the PPA salary base, and earn ITCs under s. 127(9). Work under s. 37(2) (outside Canada) earns no ITCs.

The taxpayer tested its Canadian-developed software on a mainframe computer owned by Mantissa Corp. and physically located in Birmingham, Alabama. The Minister sought to split the project geographically, relegating mainframe costs to s. 37(2) (the Mantissa payments of $63,516 and $165,157), while allowing the testing salaries under s. 37(1); the communication charges were disallowed separately because of the proxy election.

Holistic Activity Integration & Locus of Human Agency: Following Tigney, Justice Lamarre held that the testing was part of an interrelated set of activities collectively necessary to advance the software in Canada. The Tax Court in LGL Limited distinguished Data Kinetics because no personnel went to the U.S., but the Federal Court of Appeal in LGL Limited expressly disagreed with Data Kinetics, holding that each expenditure must be tested for whether the SR&ED to which it relates was carried on in Canada.

Proxy Method — Lease of Equipment vs. Overhead: Under the proxy method, indirect overhead is replaced by the PPA. Direct deductions for non-salary/non-material items are restricted to the "lease of premises, facilities or equipment".

The taxpayer claimed $26,203 paid to Unitel for a dedicated Ottawa–Birmingham telephone line as "communication charges". The Minister disallowed the amount because of the proxy election, arguing that it was attributable to the use of the leased mainframe (and therefore overhead covered by the PPA) and that the line was general office equipment.

Tangible Chattel Lease Substance Test: A "lease" requires a contract granting the right to possess, use, and enjoy tangible personal property for a specified period for rent. The provision does not distinguish payments for the use of the mainframe from payments for the line carrying data to and from it; because the line was used solely for, and formed a necessary part of, the SR&ED, the charges were for a valid "lease of equipment" under cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B).
ITA cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) & (VI)

Exclusion of General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF): Leased equipment under the proxy method cannot consist of general purpose office equipment or furniture (which is subsumed under the PPA).
Telecommunications lines and office communication links are presumptively treated by CRA auditors as general office utilities or GPOEF-adjacent administrative infrastructure.

Specialized Technical Architecture Standard: The Court found the line was not general purpose office equipment because both parties admitted it was used solely to transmit data to and from the Mantissa mainframe and it formed a necessary part of the SR&ED activity; the decision did not require proof of specialized optoelectronic hardware (that rationale appears in CRA Lease Expenditures Policy s. 4.3.1). The expenditure was thus wholly attributable to equipment or facilities used for SR&ED testing, rather than general office telephony or standard commercial internet.
ITA cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) & (VI) (Post-Dec 15, 2024 Rules)

Operating Time Thresholds (ASA or Primarily): Leased equipment must be used ASA (90% or more) for SR&ED in Canada (100% claimable) or primarily (more than 50%) for SR&ED in Canada (50% claimable). (Note: Lease eligibility was excluded for 2014–Dec 15, 2024 under subpara. 37(8)(d)(ii) and reinstated after Dec 15, 2024).

Not at issue in Data Kinetics: the mainframe was accessed under a written agreement with Mantissa effective November 1, 1991, for a monthly fee, and both parties admitted the line was used solely for transmitting data to and from the mainframe; under the post-Dec 15, 2024 rules, however, a lack of usage records separating SR&ED from non-SR&ED use would expose a lease claim to allocation challenges.

Contemporaneous Utilization Evidence: The claimant bears the burden of proving via lease contracts, system logbooks, and network/CPU utilization records that the dedicated line and mainframe lease operating time met the ASA or primarily thresholds for SR&ED in Canada.
Directly Engaged Salaries and Wages: Under the proxy method, only salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada are deductible and eligible for the PPA base.
Not in dispute in Data Kinetics: the Minister allowed the wages and salaries of employees working on testing under s. 37(1); only the Mantissa mainframe payments were reallocated to s. 37(2).

Physical Locus of the Employee Performing Testing: The Court found that the testing was performed by the software development team in Canada, with all instructions and data directed from Canada and the results returned to Canada for analysis; the salaries themselves had been allowed by the Minister under s. 37(1) and were not before the Court.
ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) vs. cl. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B); Reg. 2900(2)(c)

Travel, Lodging & Reimbursed Customer-Site Testing Costs: Under the proxy method, travel/lodging is excluded overhead. Under the traditional method, travel/lodging for testing in Canada must be "directly related" and "incremental" to SR&ED and not reimbursed.

Claiming customer-site testing travel and lodging under the proxy method, or claiming testing expenses that were reimbursed by customers, may trigger disallowance under the proxy-method overhead exclusion (CRA Overhead Policy s. 2.0) or reductions for third-party reimbursement; neither issue arose in Data Kinetics.

Strict Method Election & Incremental Unreimbursed Nexus: Travel/lodging for customer-site testing is barred under the proxy method (covered by PPA). Under the traditional method, it is allowable only with job-costing proof of direct linkage, incrementality, and zero third-party reimbursement.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian corporate taxpayers and their advisors can pre-emptively neutralize the audit triggers, territorial severance arguments, and proxy-method disallowances identified in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, the following two applied case studies model contemporary Canadian SR&ED projects. Both case studies incorporate the governing statutory framework of the Income Tax Act, including the post-December 15, 2024 legislative restoration of SR&ED lease expenditures under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI), as well as the CRA's current Lease Expenditures Policy and Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Mainframe Middleware and Financial Cryptography — Structuring Cross-Border Compute Leases and Dedicated Optoelectronic Bandwidth Under the Proxy Method
Industry Context and Project Scenario

Chronos Ledger Systems Inc. ("Chronos"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Kanata (Ottawa), Ontario, is developing an ultra-low-latency, lock-free distributed memory-table architecture designed to process cryptographic zero-knowledge (ZK) state transitions on enterprise IBM zSystems mainframes. The core technological uncertainty centres on whether Chronos's proprietary speculative concurrency-control algorithm can prevent non-linear cache-coherency degradation and memory-bus deadlocks when executing across a 32-way coupled mainframe Sysplex at transaction rates exceeding 1.2 million operations per second. While all software engineering, mathematical modelling, and source-code compilation take place at Chronos's Ottawa laboratory by eight full-time Canadian software architects (earning $1,100,000 in eligible SR&ED salaries), Chronos does not own a 32-way coupled mainframe cluster in Canada.

To execute its experimental benchmark runs during its taxation year ending December 31, 2025 (following the December 15, 2024 reinstatement of lease expenditure eligibility), Chronos enters into an arrangement with Vulcan Mainframe Corp. ("Vulcan"), a US corporation located in Birmingham, Alabama, which houses the exact IBM mainframe topology required. To stream high-volume transactional state telemetry between Ottawa and Birmingham without public-internet packet jitter skewing the latency measurements, Chronos procures a dedicated point-to-point Layer-1 optical wavelength circuit from a telecommunications carrier for $96,000 per year, alongside $140,000 paid to Vulcan for mainframe access. Chronos elects to file Form T661 using the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act.
The Unremediated Audit Pitfalls

Without proactive legal and technical structuring, Chronos faces three severe disallowances upon CRA audit review that mirror the exact dispute in Data Kinetics. First, Chronos's accounting department records the $96,000 telecommunications invoice under General Ledger Account 6420 ("Internet & Telecommunications Utilities") based on a standard carrier "Master Services Agreement." The CRA Financial Reviewer disallows the entire $96,000 expenditure, asserting that internet and telephone service charges are indirect overhead replaced by the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Section 4.7.1 of the Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy.

Second, the contract with Vulcan is titled a "Managed Mainframe Testing and Benchmarking Agreement," under which Vulcan's US systems engineers occasionally reboot partitions and configure job-control scripts. Relying on the Minister's geographic splitting argument in Data Kinetics and the Federal Court of Appeal's strict territoriality rule in LGL Limited, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) determines that the testing phase occurred physically in Alabama. Consequently, the CRA reclassifies the $140,000 Vulcan payment and 35% of Chronos's Ottawa engineering salaries ($385,000 attributable to test execution) from subsection 37(1) to subsection 37(2), stripping Chronos of all 35% enhanced refundable ITCs and corresponding PPA base inclusions on those amounts. Third, neither the optical carrier contract nor the Vulcan arrangement tracks the exact percentage of total operating hours devoted to SR&ED versus commercial customer demonstrations, failing the substantiation standards of Section 5.1 of the Lease Expenditures Policy.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan

To bring the entire testing phase squarely within Justice Lamarre's holding in Data Kinetics—and insulate it against the LGL Limited foreign-activity severance rule—Chronos must first establish an Ottawa-centric execution governance protocol. Under this governance framework, Chronos must contractually and operationally prohibit Vulcan's US personnel from writing test scripts, modifying configuration parameters, compiling code, or analyzing output logs. All system administration, Logical Partition (LPAR) provisioning, job submission via Job Control Language (JCL) scripts, and telemetry ingestion must be executed exclusively via remote command consoles operated by Chronos's engineers physically seated at terminals in Ottawa, Ontario. In the Form T661 technical narrative (Part 2, Lines 242–246), Chronos must frame the Alabama mainframe runs not as a standalone testing project, but as an iterative, closed-loop feedback mechanism integrated into the daily Ottawa algorithm-design cycle—mirroring Justice Lamarre's finding that the remote mainframe testing was part of a set of interrelated activities that collectively were necessary to the advancement of the SR&ED that was carried on in Canada.

In the second phase of restructuring, Chronos's tax counsel must redraft both the telecommunications agreement and the Vulcan mainframe agreement prior to execution to satisfy the strict legal definition of a "lease of equipment" under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI). Specifically, counsel must replace the generic "Bandwidth Services Agreement" with a Dedicated Optoelectronic Equipment and Wavelength Lease Agreement. Tracking the Black's Law Dictionary definition of lease quoted in Data Kinetics and Section 4.3.1 of the CRA's Lease Expenditures Policy, the contract must explicitly grant Chronos the exclusive right to possess, control, use, and enjoy specified tangible personal property for a stipulated term in exchange for periodic rent. Schedule "A" to the lease must itemize the dedicated physical optoelectronic hardware allocated to Chronos, including Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) optical transponders in Ottawa, dedicated dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) line cards, optical amplifiers, and dedicated switching ports, explicitly stating that the equipment is dedicated point-to-point infrastructure and contains no General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF). Concurrently, counsel must replace the "Managed Testing Services Agreement" with a Dedicated Mainframe LPAR Equipment Lease Agreement with Vulcan, specifying that Chronos is leasing exclusive physical processor capacity (dedicated central processors, coupling facility links, and hardware system area memory allocation) by the hour or month as a passive hardware chattel lease, with zero consulting, programming, or testing services rendered by Vulcan.

In the third phase, to satisfy the operating-time rules under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) (ASA, 90% or more) and (VI) (Primarily, more than 50%) for post-December 15, 2024 lease expenditures, Chronos must implement automated, tamper-evident telemetry logging. The engineering team must configure the Ottawa border router and optical transponder to generate Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) traffic logs recording active transmission timestamps, source and destination IP subnets, and payload hashes, while physically isolating the dedicated line from Chronos's corporate office local area network so that 100% of the bandwidth operating time is restricted to transmitting experimental test builds and telemetry between the Ottawa lab and the Birmingham mainframe. Simultaneously, Chronos must extract IBM System Management Facilities (SMF) Type 30 and Type 70 CPU accounting records for every leased time-window, linking 94% of total leased LPAR operating time directly to SR&ED experimental batch job identifiers, thereby qualifying 100% of the $140,000 lease cost under the 90% ASA threshold of subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I).

Finally, Chronos must integrate its version-control and issue-tracking repositories with employee timesheets so that every hour of the $385,000 testing salary component is mapped to a specific Ottawa workstation IP address, a numbered experimental hypothesis in the SR&ED test matrix, and the corresponding remote SMF job log transmitted over the dedicated optical line. This contemporaneous documentation proves beyond doubt that the testing salaries were incurred for work physically executed in Canada under subsection 37(1) and clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), securing 100% of the $96,000 optical lease, $140,000 mainframe lease, $1,100,000 salary pool, and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount ($605,000) for enhanced ITC generation.
Case Study 2: Aerospace Telemetry Compression Software — Remediating Customer-Site Testing Travel, Reimbursed Expenditures, and Hybrid Cross-Border Field Trials
Industry Context and Project Scenario

VectraAvionics Corp. ("Vectra"), a Canadian engineering firm based in Calgary, Alberta, is developing a real-time neural-adaptive telemetry compression engine for next-generation turbofan aircraft engines. The technological uncertainty arises from severe high-frequency acoustic vibration spectra during transonic compressor stalls, which corrupt standard lossless compression dictionaries within 5 milliseconds—requiring Vectra to develop a novel state-space predictive encoding algorithm capable of maintaining bit-error rates below 10⁻⁹ over bandwidth-constrained avionics buses.

During its 2025 taxation year, Vectra incurs $800,000 in Calgary-based SR&ED engineering salaries. However, resolving the technological uncertainty requires two external validation phases. In the first phase, involving domestic customer-site testing travel and reimbursements, Vectra's Calgary engineers travel six times to a commercial aircraft manufacturer's propulsion test cell in Mississauga, Ontario, to test the algorithm on live engine test stands, incurring $65,000 in airfare and lodging within Canada. Under a commercial development agreement, the Mississauga customer reimburses Vectra $25,000 toward these travel and on-site testing costs. In the second phase, involving cross-border test-stand integration, extreme icing-wind-tunnel propulsion data can only be generated at a specialized facility in Huntsville, Alabama; consequently, Vectra dispatches two Calgary engineers to Alabama for four weeks (incurring $32,000 in salaries while physically in Alabama and $18,000 in US travel and lodging) to manually calibrate sensors and run code compilations on-site, rather than streaming the data back to Calgary. Vectra's controller prepares a draft SR&ED claim electing the Proxy Method, claiming the full $800,000 in salaries (including the $32,000 earned while physically in Alabama), the $65,000 in domestic testing travel and lodging, and the $18,000 in US travel and lodging.
The Unremediated Audit Pitfalls

If filed as drafted, Vectra's claim will suffer three cascading audit adjustments directly governed by Data Kinetics, LGL Limited, and Section 4.7.2 of the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. First, applying the proxy-method overhead exclusion (Section 2.0) together with Section 4.7.2 of the Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, the CRA will disallow the entire $83,000 in testing travel and lodging ($65,000 domestic and $18,000 US). Because Vectra elected the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), travel and lodging expenditures are deemed indirect overhead subsumed within the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and cannot be claimed on Form T661.

Second, even if Vectra had elected the traditional method, the $25,000 reimbursed by the Mississauga customer reduces qualified expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9), and triggers an immediate audit inquiry into whether the Mississauga trips constituted routine commercial Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) rather than eligible SR&ED. Third, because two engineers physically travelled to Alabama to execute code compilations and sensor calibrations on foreign soil, Vectra loses the legal protection of Data Kinetics (where all employees remained in Canada) and falls squarely under the Federal Court of Appeal's territorial disallowance in LGL Limited. Furthermore, pursuant to Sections 6.1 and 6.3 of the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, overhead and travel related to SR&ED work performed outside Canada must be segregated and excluded from subsection 37(1), including travel, hotel, and meal costs related to salary or wages that are deemed under the subsection 37(1.4) permissible salary rules to be for SR&ED carried on in Canada.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan

Before the statutory filing deadline for Form T661 (18 months after the end of the taxation year), Vectra's tax advisor must first conduct a rigorous quantitative method-election modelling analysis comparing the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) against the Traditional Method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c). Under the Proxy Method, the $65,000 in Canadian testing travel and lodging is permanently non-deductible as a specific SR&ED expenditure and earns zero direct ITCs because the PPA replaces all overhead. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, Section 4.7.2 of the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy explicitly allows expenses for travel to and lodging in Canada to perform testing at a customer location as "SR&ED overhead and other expenditures" on Line 360 of Form T661, provided they satisfy the two-pronged statutory test of Regulation 2900(2)(c): first, the expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada with no intervening step; and second, the expenditure must be incremental, meaning it would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred. Where Vectra also incurs substantial dedicated facility utility costs, specialized consumable supplies, and incremental testing travel that collectively exceed the notional PPA (or where Vectra prioritizes deducting actual overhead amounts in its Section 37 pool, given that the notional PPA cannot be deducted in computing income for tax purposes), electing the Traditional Method recovers the Canadian testing travel and lodging. If, however, the PPA exceeds total actual incremental overhead, Vectra should retain the Proxy Method and strictly exclude all travel and lodging from Line 360 to prevent audit adjustments.

In the second step of remediation, Vectra must contractually unbundle its customer reimbursements and segregate its SR&ED testing protocols to satisfy Section 4.7.2 of the Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. Counsel should amend the commercial agreement with the Mississauga aircraft manufacturer to eliminate the $25,000 expense reimbursement clause for experimental testing travel, restructuring the payment schedule instead around fixed-price commercial supply milestones for the final certified avionics module. Simultaneously, a separate Research and Experimental Testing Access Addendum should stipulate that pre-certification experimental trials conducted by Vectra on the Mississauga test stand are undertaken at Vectra's sole financial risk and expense to resolve Vectra's internal technological uncertainties, with Vectra retaining full intellectual property ownership. In parallel, Vectra must establish distinct project phase codes in its job-costing ledger—as mandated by the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy—cleanly separating Phase I Experimental Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation (SR&ED claimable) from Phase II Customer Factory Acceptance Testing (non-SR&ED commercial cost).

In the third step, Vectra must re-engineer its cross-border testing in Huntsville, Alabama, into remote Canadian execution so as to restore the judicial shield of Data Kinetics and avoid severance under LGL Limited. Instead of dispatching two Calgary engineers to reside in Alabama for four weeks to compile code and analyze telemetry on-site, Vectra must replicate the exact operational architecture validated by Justice Lamarre in Data Kinetics. Vectra should arrange for the Alabama facility technicians to mount the standard sensor harness onto the engine, while Vectra leases a dedicated point-to-point encrypted satellite or fibre telemetry link—an eligible post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease under proxy subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) or traditional subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)—connecting the Huntsville test cell directly to Vectra's Calgary laboratory. By keeping the two Calgary engineers physically at their consoles in Calgary to transmit all real-time adaptive compression parameters, trigger test runs, and analyze the incoming vibration bitstreams in Canada, the human experimental workforce remains entirely inside Canada, and 100% of the $32,000 engineering salary and the leased data link qualify as "SR&ED carried on in Canada" under subsection 37(1) pursuant to Data Kinetics. For any brief, unavoidable physical presence in Alabama—such as a three-day trip by one Canadian-resident engineer solely to verify physical sensor calibration that cannot be performed in Canada—Vectra must ensure that the engineer's foreign-situated salary remains strictly within the 10% permissible salary limit of total Canadian SR&ED salaries under subsection 37(1.4), accounting for any related overhead in strict compliance with Section 6.3 of the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy.

In the final step, Vectra must implement a granular job-costing system linking every domestic travel voucher, hotel folio, and remote link invoice directly to a numbered Experimental Test Plan (ETP). Each ETP must contemporaneously record the specific acoustic-stall compression hypothesis tested during that trip or remote session, the exact hours of test-stand and dedicated-link operating time confirming 90% or greater ASA usage for SR&ED, a signed accounting certification that no customer reimbursement applied to the cost code, and the quantitative analysis of bit-error rates generated in Calgary, thereby satisfying both the technical threshold of subsection 248(1) and the financial linkage requirements of Section 37.
Summary Comparison of Remedial Restructuring Across Both Case Studies

The following table synthesizes the structural, contractual, and evidentiary interventions applied across both industry case studies to satisfy the statutory standards established in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen and subsequent CRA policies.

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Practice Directives

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen remains an indispensable precedent for Canadian tax counsel and technical SR&ED advisors. While Justice Lamarre's decision delivered a decisive victory for the taxpayer—confirming that remote testing conducted from Canadian terminals on a foreign mainframe via a dedicated telecommunications link constitutes SR&ED "carried on in Canada" under subsection 37(1), and establishing that dedicated bandwidth charges represent a valid "lease of equipment" (the optoelectronic-equipment rationale being the CRA's later gloss in its Lease Expenditures Policy rather than part of the judgment) under the proxy method—subsequent judicial and administrative developments require disciplined execution to secure those benefits.

First, following the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in LGL Limited v. The Queen, claimants can no longer rely on a loose "project as a whole" argument to shelter physical activities conducted outside Canada under subsection 37(1). Because the Federal Court of Appeal in LGL Limited expressly stated that it could not agree with Data Kinetics (which the Tax Court in LGL Limited had distinguished only because no personnel went to the U.S.), to draw any support from Data Kinetics, the claimant's evidentiary record must prove that all human intellectual and experimental agency occurred within Canada, and that the foreign component was strictly limited to passive hardware accessed remotely via telecommunications infrastructure. Second, with Parliament's restoration of SR&ED lease expenditure eligibility for costs incurred after December 15, 2024, Justice Lamarre's chattel-lease analysis of dedicated bandwidth and remote compute equipment has regained immediate statutory force under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI), as explicitly recognized in Section 4.3.1 of the CRA's revised Lease Expenditures Policy. By drafting explicit equipment leases that exclude general purpose office equipment, maintaining automated system logs substantiating the 90% (ASA) or 50% (primarily) operating-time thresholds, and carefully modelling the treatment of testing-related travel and reimbursements between the traditional and proxy methods, Canadian taxpayers can structure audit-proof SR&ED claims that withstand both administrative scrutiny and judicial review.
